text.eyebrow: The cedi and prices · to August 2026
text.lede: When a dollar costs 10% more cedis, imported goods cost about 3% more within three months and about 5% more within a year. Local goods follow almost as much, about 4% within a year, so a weaker cedi raises prices well beyond imports. GSS's split between imported and local goods starts in 2021, so this runs from February 2021 to August 2026, and it is recomputed with each release.
text.tile-0-l: of a fall in the cedi has reached imported-goods prices after three months
text.tile-2-l: for local goods after a year
text.tile-3-l: between the cedi's moves and import inflation, at the closest fit (1–3 months fit almost as well)
text.s1-h2: Import inflation follows the cedi, about two months behind
text.s1-p1: Over a year, import inflation moves most closely with the cedi's change over the year ending two months earlier (a correlation of 0.87; one to three months fit almost as well). Each 10% rise in cedis per dollar goes with about 4.5 more points of import inflation two months later. The cedi's fall peaked in November 2022, when a dollar cost 121% more cedis than a year before. Import inflation peaked two months later, at 62.4% in January 2023. After the cedi's strongest month in the 2025 recovery, June 2025, import inflation kept falling for nine months, to −0.6% in March 2026: the only month in this record when imported goods cost less than a year before.
text.s1-p2: In August 2026 a dollar cost 5.1% more cedis than a year earlier. Imported goods cost 2.2% more than a year earlier, and local goods 6.2% more.
text.c1-cap: Change on a year earlier, %, January 2022 to August 2026. Cedis per US dollar: the Bank of Ghana's interbank mid-rate, averaged over each month; a rise means the cedi fell. Imported and local goods: GSS's consumer price index by origin. Hover or tap for any month; Cedi moved two months later slides the cedi's line along to show the lag.
text.c2-cap: Correlation between prices' change over a year and the cedi's change over the year ending 0 to 15 months earlier, January 2022 to August 2026. Highest at two months for both imported and local goods.
text.s2-h2: About half of a fall reaches import prices within a year
text.s2-p1: Set each month's change in import prices against the cedi's change in that month and in each of the twelve before, and the share passed on builds up like this: 7% in the same month, 20% after one month, 32% after three. Then it slows: 36% after six months and 51% after a year. Local goods follow a similar path, to 44%, and all items to 46%. With five and a half years of data the range is wide: 39–63% after a year for imported goods.
text.c3-cap: Share of a change in cedis per US dollar that has reached prices, by months since the change, %. Shaded: the 90% range for imported goods. Monthly changes, February 2021 to August 2026 (67 months), with each calendar month's usual change taken out.
text.s3-h2: The cedi's three big moves since 2022
text.s3-p1: In the 2022 crash a dollar went from 6.01 to 13.07 cedis, and over the year from January 2022 imported goods rose 62.4%, more than the 40.4% rise the model above predicts. World prices of fuel and food also surged in 2022, and this analysis doesn't separate them from the cedi. In the 2024 slide (11.65 to 15.99 cedis), imported goods rose 18.0%, less than the 27.9% rise the model predicts. In the 2025 recovery (15.53 back down to 10.28 cedis), they fell 0.6%, close to the 2.6% fall the model predicts.

text.t-ep-cap: Prices: change over the twelve months from the start month. Cedis per dollar: monthly averages, at the start and at the cedi's turning point. Predicted: what the model behind the chart above gives for imported goods over the same twelve months, from the cedi's moves plus the usual rise in prices that has nothing to do with the cedi.
text.k-cur-sub: euro, yuan and a basket, after a year
text.k-cur: Measured against the euro, 50% of a fall reaches import prices within a year; against the Chinese yuan, 58%; against a basket of the three (half dollar, a quarter each euro and yuan), 54%. The answer barely depends on the currency.
text.k-w22: From March 2023, once the crash had passed through (42 months), the share after a year is 34%, and it builds more slowly: 16% after three months. The 2022 crash pulls the average up.
text.k-asym-sub: of a fall / of a rise, after three months
text.k-asym: After three months, 38% of a fall in the cedi has reached import prices, but only 17% of a rise. After a year the two are close: 46% and 44%. Prices go up faster than they come down. Only 17 of the 67 months saw a stronger cedi, so this is the least certain result here.
text.k-long-sub: all items after a year, 1998 to 2026
text.k-long: All-items prices go back to 1998. Over 1998 to 2026 (328 months), 43% of a fall in the cedi reaches them within a year; over 1998 to 2020, 42%; since 2021, 46%. The recent years aren't unusual.
text.m-data: The cedi. The Bank of Ghana's interbank mid-rate for the US dollar, averaged over each month, in today's cedis. Months with fewer than 10 published rates, and the month in progress, are left out. Prices. GSS's consumer price index for imported goods, local goods and all items: StatsBank before January 2022 for imported and local goods (January 2021 for all items), then the monthly CPI annex, which agrees with StatsBank to its rounding where both exist. Only values that pass TARIN's checks are used.
text.m-how: How much, how fast. Each month's change in prices (in logs) is regressed on the change in cedis per dollar in the same month and in each of the twelve before, with a dummy for each calendar month. The running sum of the cedi's coefficients is the share passed on after that many months. Standard errors are Newey–West with four lags; the shaded range is 1.645 of them either side, a 90% range. How many months later. The correlation between prices' change over a year and the cedi's change over the year ending k months earlier, for k from 0 to 15.
